A set partition is said to be ordered if the blocks of the partition are listed in a specific order. The ordered set partitions of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with a unique minimal element adjoined, form a lattice $\Om_n$ with respect to refinement. The lattice $\Om_n$ is well known to be the face lattice of the permutohedron. In this paper we study the combinatorics and topology of two subposets of $\Om_n$ with restricted block sizes, either all divisible by some fixed $d\ge2$, or all congruent to $1$ modulo $d$. For the $d$-divisible case we derive an explicit recursive atom ordering for the lattice, as well as formulas for the action of the symmetric group on the Whitney homology and the rank-selected homology, and also for the multiplicity of the trivial representation. In the 1 mod $d$ case we show that the poset has a curious interval structure related to the $k$-Catalan numbers. Our investigations lead to enumerative invariants in both cases. Open problems and avenues for future research are scattered throughout.

L53@P1: 1.1 Contributions of this work
L54@P1: In this article, we focus on a novel approach for the feature embedding of sequencing
L55@P1: reads. Differently from the works proposed in the literature which essentially consist
L56@P1: of elaborate applications of NLP techniques, we propose a theoretical investigation of
L57@P1: combinatorial properties that would guarantee compact embedded representations of the
L58@P1: sequences while preserving similarities. In this section, we provide a discussion on the
L59@P1: motivations; then, we give an overall description of the proposed method, and finally we
L60@P1: present our main contributions.
L61@P1: Motivations. The main question addressed in this paper is whether there exists a
L62@P1: “similarity signature” that can be: (i) easily detected while reading the sequence, and
L63@P1: (ii) used to define an effective feature embedding method. We answer to this question
L64@P1: by exploiting one of the most well-known factorizations in combinatorics on words: the
L65@P1: Lyndon factorization [12, 13]. Such a factorization has some main desired properties: (i)
L66@P1: it is unique for a word, (ii) it can be computed in linear time, and more recently, it has
L67@P1: been proved in [1, 14] that, under some conditions, the sequence of Lyndon factors of a
L68@P1: word shares consecutive common factors with the Lyndon factorization of a superstring
L69@P1: of the word itself. The notion of Lyndon word is not novel in the field of Bioinformatics,
L70@P1-2: 2since it was used to locate short motifs [15] and more recently it was explored in the
L71@P2: development of the bijective Burrows-Wheeler Transforms [16].
L72@P2: Surprisingly, we discovered that the sequence of lengths of the factors in Lyndon
L73@P2: factorizations is enough to capture sequence similarity, thus allowing the definition of a
L74@P2: word signature, called fingerprint.
L75@P2: Proposed method. In this paper we propose a novel feature embedding method for
L76@P2: sequences generated by sequencing, called reads, that exploits the fingerprint of such
L77@P2: sequences to produce their embedded representations. To the best of our knowledge, it
L78@P2: represents the first attempt to build a feature representation that is based on theoretical
L79@P2: combinatorial properties proved to capture sequence similarities and also suitable for
L80@P2: machine learning approaches.

L83@P2: Lyndon-based feature embeddings of sequencing reads.

L85@P2: training on a text corpus, but it is based on combinatorial properties that capture
L86@P2: sequence similarities. In Sections 3.1 and 4, we investigate properties of the

L106@P2-3: 32 Related work
L107@P3: The past years have seen impressive advances in sequence mining. State-of-the-art
L108@P3: sequence mining methods could be categorized as follows: (i) sequence alignment [17], (ii)
L109@P3: string kernels [18], (iii) time-series classification [19, 20], and (iv) pattern discovery [21, 22].
L110@P3: In the following, we will focus on the feature embedding of sequencing reads.
L111@P3: Recent results in NLP [7] identify terms with a similar linguistic context by exploiting
L112@P3: word embedding. In this approach, known as word2vec, words or phrases are mapped to
L113@P3: vectors of real numbers in a low-dimensional space. By training a neural network over a
L114@P3: large text corpus, words with similar linguistic context correspond to vectors that are
L115@P3: close points in the Euclidean space.
L116@P3: In [5] the word2vec framework is applied to extract features from biological sequences.
L117@P3: The embeddings generated for general biological sequences are named BioVec for genomic
L118@P3: sequence and ProtVec for proteins. The tool seq2vec [6] extends the idea proposed
L119@P3: in [5] by modeling a sequence as a sentence in a text corpus while k-mers derived from
L120@P3: such a sequence are words in the sentence given as input to the embedding algorithm.
L121@P3: In [23], a novel model for fast classification of sequencing reads is proposed, which is
L122@P3: named fastDNA. It is based on FastText [24], which is an extension of word2vec, where
L123@P3: the main difference is that instead of using individual words to train the Neural Network,
L124@P3: words are broken into several n-grams used to train the network.
L125@P3: In [25], another well-known NLP model, the Bidirectional Encoder Representations
L126@P3: from Transformers (BERT), is adapted to model DNA general embeddings. The result is
L127@P3: DNABERT, a novel pre-trained bidirectional representation encoder for DNA-language.
L128@P3: These sequence embedding methods essentially consist of elaborate applications of
L129@P3: NLP techniques, in which an embedding model is first trained on a large text corpus,
L130@P3: and then used to transform biological sequences into numeric vectors to be used by
L131@P3: learning algorithms. Therefore, the computational space and time required to embed a
L132@P3: sequence dataset is a critical issue of these embedding methods. Instead, in our approach
L133@P3: we change perspective: we investigate combinatorial properties that would guarantee
L134@P3: compact embedding representations able to preserve similarities. As a result, we define
L135@P3: novel embedding representations which can be computed, for each sequence, in linear
L136@P3: time with respect to the length of the sequence itself, without requiring any previous
L137@P3: training. Furthermore, the ability to capture sequence similarities can be controlled by
L138@P3: tuning some parameters that are determined by the specific factorization used.
